prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Construction Spending
Description: Provides monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. The data is collected through the Value of Construction Put in Place Survey (VIP) and covers construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research Report: Construction Spending (Value of Construction Put in Place)

## 1. Verification of the dataset description

The description you provided is accurate and matches the Census Bureau's official program description nearly verbatim. The program is published by the **U.S. Census Bureau** (an agency of the U.S. Department of Commerce) under the name **Construction Spending**, also known as the **Value of Construction Put in Place Survey (VIP)** — BEA and other agencies sometimes call it "VPIP" — and its data series is designated **C30**. It is one of the Census Bureau's Principal Economic Indicators.

- Program homepage: https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/c30index.html
- About the survey: https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/about_the_survey.html
- Methodology: https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/methodology.html
- Definitions: https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/definitions.html

## 2. Publisher and governance

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, Economic Indicators Division (Construction Expenditures Branch). Contact: econ.indicators@census.gov.
- **Parent organization:** U.S. Department of Commerce. Congress funds the Bureau via the Commerce-Justice-Science appropriations subcommittees and oversees it through the Senate Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs and House Oversight committees (per CRS report R47847).
- **Statutory framework:** The Bureau itself dates to 1902 and moved to Commerce in 1913; its statistical authorities were codified as Title 13, U.S. Code, in 1954 (68 Stat. 1012).

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

- **Collection authority:** Title 13, U.S. Code, **Sections 131 and 182** authorize the Census Bureau to conduct the survey and request voluntary assistance from respondents.
- **Confidentiality:** Under **Title 13, Section 9**, respondent reports are confidential, usable only for statistical purposes, and copies retained in respondents' files are immune from legal process.
- **Participation is voluntary** — unlike the decennial census or ACS, this is not a mandatory-response survey under 13 U.S.C. Chapter 7.
- **Other governing statutes:** The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (OMB clearance for the forms; OMB control no. 0607-0607) and the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018, which shape federal statistical practice generally.

## 4. History

- **1915–1964:** The U.S. Department of Labor collected construction value data; some annual publications survive from this era.
- **1964:** The Census Bureau took over the program and began collecting what became the VIP series (Census/Census-hosted webinar transcript, March 2014: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/econ/events/business-economy/03-12-2014/transcript_vip.pdf).
- **1993:** A major reclassification of construction types occurred; monthly data on the current classification begins **January 1993**. Data before 1993 are *not comparable* to the current series.
- **August 1, 2003:** The old (1964-based) classification system and the **constant-dollar (inflation-adjusted) series** were discontinued. Historical 1964–2002 data under the old classification remain available at https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/oldtc.html.
- The sampling frame's historical continuity is notable: projects have been selected from **Dodge** construction reports (F.W. Dodge / McGraw-Hill, now Dodge Data & Analytics) since the program's early decades, supplemented by Census's own Survey of Construction and building-permit systems.

## 5. What the data measure

"Value of construction put in place" is the value of construction **installed or erected at the site** during a period, regardless of when a project started or when contractors were paid. For a project it includes:

1. Cost of materials installed or erected
2. Labor costs (contractor and force account) plus a share of construction equipment rental
3. Contractor's profit
4. Architectural and engineering work
5. Miscellaneous overhead and office costs chargeable to the project
6. Interest and taxes paid during construction (except for state/local public projects)

Notable exclusions: land acquisition and most maintenance/repair work. Projects are classified as private or public (federal, state, local) **by ownership during construction**.

## 6. Methodology (important for data scientists)

- **Target population:** All construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures, private and public, in the 50 states and D.C.
- **Data collection:** Four **Construction Progress Reporting Surveys (CPRS)** collect monthly progress reports from owners of sampled projects (~4,000 private nonresidential, ~6,500 state/local, and ~1,500 multifamily projects per month in recent years), each project staying in sample until completion. Data collection begins the day after the reference month and runs about three weeks.
- **Sampling:** Stratified systematic samples of projects valued **≥ $75,000**, drawn from **Dodge Data & Analytics (DDA)** lists plus a small sample of projects in non-permit-issuing areas; multifamily projects are subsampled from the Census Bureau's Survey of Construction. Single-family and improvements estimates are derived from the Survey of Construction and the **BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey** (which replaced the older SORAR). Federal, utilities, and railroad series are benchmarked to or derived from administrative/outside sources.
- **Estimation:** Weighted sums of project values (basic weight × outlier adjustment × A/E and miscellaneous cost adjustment × frame duplication factor). Variance estimated with a **stratified jackknife** procedure; standard errors/CVs are published.
- **Benchmarking:** Private manufacturing estimates are periodically benchmarked to the Census Bureau's **Annual Capital Expenditures Survey (ACES)** (done for 1992, 1994, 1998, 2003, 2008, 2012, and 2017).

**Known limitations and critiques** (worth flagging for any analyst):
- Heavy reliance on the **private Dodge frame** creates potential coverage bias, partially corrected by upward adjustments whose accuracy degrades over time (Census methodology documents acknowledge this).
- **High imputation rates**: a 2023 Federal Reserve FEDS Note found roughly **70% of 2021 private nonresidential spending was imputed** for nonresponding projects, and argued the imputation cap (101.5% of estimated cost) likely **understated** nonresidential spending during the pandemic-era cost surge — real spending may have been as much as ~20% higher in 2022 Q3 than published (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/nonresidential-construction-spending-is-likely-not-as-weak-as-it-seems-20230324.html).
- A 2025 BEA working paper (WP2025-8) documents persistent gaps between VIP-based and ACES/ASM-based estimates of nonresidential structures investment.
- The series is **nominal only** (constant dollars discontinued in 2003); users must deflate it themselves (e.g., with BLS PPIs, as BEA does).

## 7. Data products, geography, and schedule

- **Frequency/units:** Monthly estimates in millions of dollars, both **not seasonally adjusted** and **seasonally adjusted annual rates (SAAR)**; annual totals also published.
- **Detail:** U.S. total; private (residential/nonresidential) and public (state & local / federal), plus roughly two dozen detailed categories (offices, healthcare, manufacturing, educational, highways, etc.).
- **Geography:** U.S. level monthly; **annual estimates by census region, division, and state** for selected categories; private manufacturing monthly at region/division level.
- **History online:** Monthly and annual data back to **1993** (current classification).
- **Release cadence:** Press release on the **first working day of each month, two months after the reference month**. Example: August 2026 data were released October 1, 2026 — total construction at a SAAR of **$2,203.1 billion**, +0.9% (±1.0%) above the revised July estimate.
- **Revision cycle:** Two months of data are revised with each release; with the May release, **88 months of seasonally adjusted data** are re-seasonally adjusted and the most recent two annual estimates are finalized; preliminary annual estimates come out with December data. A revisions analysis is published annually.

## 8. Access channels (for data librarians)

- **Official site:** census.gov/construction/c30 — current and historical press releases in PDF and Excel, "At a Glance" tables, and historical XLSX files.
- **Census API:** `https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/vip` (free API key required) — JSON time series with variables for category, data type, seasonal adjustment, and error data.
- **Interactive time series/trend charts:** https://www.census.gov/economic-indicators/econ/currentdata/?programCode=VIP
- **Data.gov catalog:** registered as a public dataset (bureau code 006:07) under a **CC0 public-domain license**.
- **FRED (St. Louis Fed):** mirrored as dozens of series, e.g., **TTLCONS** (Total Construction Spending, SAAR, 1993–present), with **ALFRED** providing historical vintages of revisions — valuable for reproducibility.
- Commercial redistributors (Moody's Analytics, Haver, Bloomberg) also carry the series; academic redistributors include the CORGIS project.

## 9. Typical users

- **Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA):** primary input for the **structures component of GDP** and as a benchmark for the construction industry in the national accounts.
- **Federal Reserve Board / FOMC staff and regional Feds:** monitoring business fixed investment and construction cycles.
- **Council of Economic Advisers, OMB, and other policy staff:** economic analysis and policy development.
- **HUD:** uses residential data to gauge the state of the nation's housing.
- **Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and mortgage/housing analysts** for residential investment trends.
- **Construction industry:** contractors, Dodge Construction Network, engineering firms, materials suppliers, and forecasters (e.g., construction analytics firms) use it for market sizing and planning.
- **Financial press and markets:** each monthly release moves coverage of the construction/economic outlook.
- **State/local governments and infrastructure policy analysts:** tracking public construction (highways, schools, water, etc.) and, recently, the on-the-ground impact of legislation such as the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and CHIPS/IRA factory-building booms.
- **Academic researchers** studying business cycles, housing, and investment.

## 10. Public benefits

- **Feeds GDP**, so it ultimately shapes the headline statistics that guide monetary and fiscal policy, Social Security indexing debates, and recession dating.
- **Timely, free, standardized, monthly** measure of a sector that historically accounts for a large swing factor in business cycles.
- **Granular public/private and category detail** lets citizens, journalists, and advocacy groups track where public infrastructure money is actually turning into built work.
- **Confidentiality protections** and voluntary cooperation demonstrate the Census model of statistical trust; the data are public-domain (CC0) and machine-readable via API.

## 11. Preservation notes

- Historical press releases (PDF/Excel) back to at least 2003 are maintained on the C30 site; **old-classification data (1964–2002)** survive as downloadable tables at the `oldtc.html` page — these are effectively a "dark archive" of the pre-1993 methodology and should be captured by anyone doing long-run historical work.
- ALFRED (St. Louis Fed) preserves **vintage revisions**, which the Census site itself does not — important because revisions (especially annual/seasonal re-benchmarkings) materially change the series.
- The 2014 Census webinar transcript is a useful primary source on program history.

## 12. Suggested citation / starting points

- U.S. Census Bureau, "Construction Spending (Value of Construction Put in Place, VIP/C30)," monthly press release, https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/
- Methodology: https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/pdf/methodology.pdf
- API: https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/vip.html

**Bottom line:** your description is correct. This is a Census Bureau economic indicator program authorized under 13 U.S.C. §§131/182, with roots in Labor Department data collection dating to 1915 and continuous Census collection since 1964 (comparable modern series since 1993), built from voluntary project-level progress surveys framed on Dodge data, feeding GDP and policy analysis nationwide — with documented methodological caveats (imputation rates, frame coverage, nominal dollars only) that sophisticated users should bear in mind.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Let me verify a few remaining items: the proposed statistical-agency reorganization, any changes to the VIP series itself, and current funding status.The search tool has reached its limit, but I can still fetch pages directly to confirm the FY2026 funding outcome.# Risk Assessment: Construction Spending / Value of Construction Put in Place (VIP)

**Scope note:** My research covers events through October 2026. One correction to my prior report: the correct OMB control number for the Construction Progress Reporting Surveys is **0607-0153** (not 0607-0607).

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- The Census Bureau's C30 site retains its complete historical archive: all monthly press releases in PDF and Excel back through at least the 1990s remain posted (https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/prpdf.html lists releases for every month of 2025 and 2026; historical data files back to 1993 remain at https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/historical_data.html), and FRED still mirrors the full series from January 1993 onward.
- However, agency-wide there were significant removals: over 3,000 pages were removed from the Census Bureau website as of February 2, 2025, "primarily articles filed under research and methodology" (Wikipedia, "United States government online resource removals under the second Trump administration"); a Jan–Feb 2025 episode following the gender-ideology executive order briefly made data platforms inaccessible (NPR, Feb. 12, 2025); and the QuickFacts tool has been down with "no short-term solution" (TPM). A 2026 tracker (dataindex.us, via The Guardian) counts at least 28 federal datasets deleted and 338 modified government-wide since January 2025.
- None of the documented removals touch the VIP/Construction Spending series or its underlying data elements; the removals hit demographic/LGBTQ research pages, methodology articles, and unrelated program tools.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** All historical VIP data files, tables, press releases, and API time series remain publicly accessible with no known alterations. The agency-wide website removals are a meaningful background risk, but no element of this dataset has been removed.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- **ICR status: Active and renewed on time.** The Construction Progress Reporting Surveys ICR (OMB 0607-0153) was approved by OIRA on **August 18, 2025** ("extension without change of a currently approved collection"), with an expiration date of **August 31, 2028** (reginfo.gov, ICR ref. 202411-0607-004; 60-day notice 89 FR 57850; 30-day notice 89 FR 90665).
- **Publication delays occurred:** The record 43-day federal government shutdown (Oct. 1 – Nov. 12, 2025) halted collection and processing. The August 2025 report, due Oct. 1, 2025, was released **Nov. 17, 2025** — roughly six weeks late (Reuters, Nov. 14, 2025; Census Bureau announcements via GovDelivery). The **February and March 2026 releases were combined and delayed**, both rescheduled to May 7, 2026 instead of April 1 and May 1 (Census press release CB26-51, March 23, 2026).
- **Since then, the schedule has normalized:** August 2026 data were released on schedule October 1, 2026 (CB26-158), and the release calendar shows a normal monthly cadence (September 2026 due Nov. 2, 2026). Collection was never skipped — only delayed — and the survey continued mailing/collecting throughout.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** Typical publication dates were missed and publication was delayed (shutdown-related), which fits the Moderate definition. The ICR is active through 2028 and the series has resumed on-time publication, so this does not rise to High Risk (no missed statutory deadline beyond the delay, no skipped collection, no expired ICR).

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- **Granularity and frequency are unchanged:** the 2025 ICR renewal was explicitly "extension without change"; no content changes to the C-700 forms were proposed (89 FR 57850). The series continues to publish the full category detail (private/public, residential/nonresidential, ~two dozen categories) at monthly frequency with the standard two-month lag, plus annual revisions and state/regional annual estimates.
- **Timeliness suffered temporarily:** the combined Feb/Mar 2026 release and multi-week shutdown delays reduced effective timeliness for roughly three reporting cycles (Oct 2025 – May 2026), but monthly cadence was restored.
- **Emerging risks:** The Census Bureau has lost ~15% of staff since FY24, faced hiring freezes and contract-approval backlogs (American Statistical Association, "The Nation's Data at Risk"; NPR, Apr. 17, 2025), and Commerce IG findings on chronic field-staff vacancies. Analysts (Marketplace, July 2025) describe statistical agencies generally "trying to preserve the quality of the headline numbers… at the expense of some of the granularity" — though documented sample cuts so far are at BLS/CPI, not VIP. The survey's pre-existing imputation-rate and Dodge-frame coverage issues (Fed FEDS Note 2023; BEA WP2025-8) could be amplified by staffing strain.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** No permanent reduction in granularity, frequency, or (after mid-2026) timeliness has occurred, so High Risk is not warranted — but realized temporary timeliness disruptions plus clear emerging risks from staffing losses and an administration-wide pattern of resource-driven statistical cuts place this above "No Known Issue."

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- **Explicit statutory authorization:** Title 13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182 are named as the legal authority on the survey forms and in every Federal Register notice for the collection (e.g., 89 FR 90665, Nov. 18, 2024). The content of what is collected is clearly specified (dollar value of construction put in place by ownership type and project class).
- **Required for implementation of a federal program:** the series is a Principal Economic Indicator and the primary input to BEA's construction components of GDP ("Construction now accounts for 7.4 percent of GDP" — Census Federal Register notice); it is used by the Federal Reserve, Treasury, and BEA for monetary and fiscal policy (FR notice; ASA letters).
- **No substitute collections exist:** the private Dodge Data & Analytics starts data are proprietary, cover starts rather than spending, and are not a public statistical substitute; BEA has documented significant gaps when alternative sources (ACES/ASM) are used instead (BEA WP2025-8).
- Caveat: no statute *mandates* publication of the monthly construction spending series specifically; Congress provides funding and the collection is voluntary for respondents.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** The statutory authorization is explicitly named, what must be collected is clear, there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes, and the data are required for implementation of a federal program (GDP/national accounts). This is among the most statutorily and programmatically anchored datasets in the federal statistical system.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- **Staffing losses exceed the 1,000-employee threshold:** the Census Bureau has lost an estimated **15% of staff since FY24** (ASA, "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025"), and Rep. Grace Meng explicitly cited "the loss of **over 1,000 Census Bureau staff** and DOGE's activities" in June 2025 (The Census Project). The bureau employed ~11,100 staff at the October 2025 shutdown, with only ~7% exempted from furlough. The FY26 President's Budget requested a further 9% staffing decline from FY24 levels (ASA; CRS IF12714).
- **Funding:** FY25 was held flat at $1.385B (a ~2.4% real purchasing-power loss); the FY26 President's Budget requested $1.677B but with the Current Surveys account *cut* ~$40M. However, **Congress's enacted FY2026 package provided ~$1.5 billion — a slight increase over FY25's $1.38 billion** (The Census Project, Jan. 7, 2026). Current Economic Statistics funding is flat at $216M. So no 10–20% budget cut materialized.
- **Leadership change:** Director Robert Santos resigned mid-term in January 2025 (AP; CRS IF11845); career Deputy Director Ron Jarmin served as acting director until **September 2025, when Trump administration official George Cook — simultaneously acting undersecretary for economic affairs, the position that oversees the bureau — took over as acting director** (NPR, Sept. 19, 2025; AP). No Senate-confirmed director has been in place since January 2025.

**Finding: High Risk.** The rubric's threshold of "1,000 or more staff lost" is met (with ~15% staffing loss), and leadership has been replaced by a political appointee after the director's departure. Funding alone would have suggested a lower rating (flat-to-slightly-up enacted budget), but the staffing and leadership criteria independently trigger High Risk.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- **No direct adverse policy action against this dataset:** the ICR renewal in August 2025 was a routine "extension without change" processed through normal PRA channels — not a Presidential Action-driven modification. There is no negative policy note on the C30 site, and the Economic Briefing Room continues to promote the indicator.
- **Proposed/pending changes affecting the statistical apparatus:** the FY2026 President's Budget "proposes to reorganize the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the Census Bureau at the Department of Commerce," with details still to be shared (ASA; CRS IF12714) — a pending structural change with uncertain implications for economic statistics. The administration discontinued at least 562 information collections between Jan. 2025 and Jan. 2026 via PRA processes, 65% more than the prior year (Chris Marcum data-integrity report), and an August 2026 Commerce Department revision quietly removed language banning political interference from its scientific-integrity policy (NPR, Aug. 31, 2026). The administration's broader data-deletion campaign (Guardian/dataindex.us tracker) has not targeted economic indicators, and Principal Economic Indicators continue to be released.
- No administration official has publicly suggested terminating or altering the Construction Spending series specifically.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** The dataset itself has not been targeted by administration policy, but proposed/pending structural changes (the BLS/BEA/Census reorganization proposal), weakened scientific-integrity protections, and an active pattern of administration-driven collection discontinuations elsewhere in government create a genuine, documented, and unresolved threat environment.

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
All historical VIP data, press releases, and API series remain fully accessible with no known alterations; agency-wide website removals have not touched this dataset.

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
The ICR is active through August 2028 and was renewed on time, but the October–November 2025 shutdown delayed the August 2025 release by ~6 weeks and forced the February/March 2026 releases to be combined and delayed to May 7, 2026; the schedule has since normalized.

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk**
Granularity and frequency are unchanged and the collection was renewed "without change," but realized (temporary) timeliness disruptions and emerging risks from a ~15% staffing loss and an administration-wide pattern of resource-driven statistical degradation warrant concern.

**Statutory Context: No Known Issue**
Explicit Title 13 U.S.C. §§131/182 authority, clearly specified content, no viable substitute data collection, and an essential role in BEA's GDP estimates anchor this dataset firmly.

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk**
Over 1,000 Census Bureau staff lost (~15% since FY24), a hiring freeze, and a leadership change (director's resignation followed by installation of a Trump political appointee as acting director) meet the High Risk thresholds, even though enacted FY26 funding slightly increased.

**Policy: Moderate Risk**
No adverse action against this dataset specifically and a routine ICR renewal, but the proposed BLS/BEA/Census reorganization, weakened scientific-integrity policy language, and the administration's pattern of PRA-based collection terminations constitute proposed or pending changes with potential to affect the program.

**Overall assessment:** The Construction Spending dataset is one of the more resilient federal datasets — statutorily anchored, GDP-critical, with intact history and a renewed ICR — but it sits inside an agency experiencing high staffing/leadership risk and moderate policy and operational turbulence, which has already manifested in shutdown-driven publication delays.
